endorsements.quote: Any substantive model update should trigger structured reverification in simulation before the system resumes patient‐facing tasks, whether the update was initiated by the manufacturer under a predetermined change control plan (PCCP; an FDA mechanism described later) or configured locally, and the scope of reverification should be proportional to the scope of the change.

This boundary supports physician‐led integration: final diagnostic and therapeutic authority remains with the supervising rheumatologist within the multidisciplinary care team, and patients should never be redirected to unsupervised robotic care.
Because such systems change through versioned updates, advancement cannot be a one‐time determination.

The institution and its faculty govern every stage, much as they do for fellows: setting standards, granting task‐specific privileges, reviewing every software update, and retaining the authority to suspend privileges at any time.

The profession should define standards for data provenance, auditability, and explainability in rheumatology‐specific AI applications, grounded in medical professionalism and patient safety, rather than leaving these decisions to vendors or regulators.

Federal regulation governs the patient‐facing stages because a humanoid system performing clinical tasks would, in regulatory terms, be a medical device; FDA authorization is required before any patient contact.
A multidisciplinary AI oversight committee (clinician educators, engineers, informaticists, ethicists, risk managers, and patient representatives) serves the equivalent role
Liability divides along familiar lines: the physician for clinical decisions, the institution for deployment and privileging, the manufacturer for device failure

Following institutional review and governance approval, humanoid trainees could initially shadow inpatient rounds and outpatient clinics without active participation while training extensively in high‐fidelity simulation.
A task progresses to indirect supervision only after sustained, documented safe performance of that specific task.
Performs standardized simulated tasks (eg, collecting a structured history) accurately and consistently, meeting benchmarks set in advance
audit logging of every patient interaction so that any output can be traced and reviewed
each stage is entered only through a gate of independently verified readiness criteria (Table 1 ).
Transparency and consent are essential, and the relevant evidence base extends beyond general attitudes toward medical AI.
We therefore identify equity monitoring as an explicit obligation of any oversight structure.

unlisted_practices: Never allow AI systems to graduate to independent practice; keep them under permanent physician supervision.
Permanently reserve communicating a final diagnosis, goals-of-care and end-of-life discussions, and ethically complex decisions to human clinicians.
Provide patients a genuine, penalty-free option to decline participation in care involving humanoid or embodied AI systems.
Process protected health information on-device when feasible so it stays local rather than being transmitted.
Prohibit secondary commercial use of clinically collected data without explicit patient consent and governance review.
Use simulated or de-identified data exclusively in early phases before any patient-facing activity.
Use multi-institutional consortia, leasing models, and shared infrastructure to reduce cost barriers so under-resourced programs can access clinical AI.
Adopt a governance structure that pairs external regulatory authorization of the device with local institutional privileging for specific tasks.

screen.reason: This is a framework and anticipatory governance commentary exploring how embodied humanoid AI systems could be trained, supervised, and governed within rheumatology clinical practice.
